title: Security Fundamentals for Java Developers knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Security Fundamentals for Java Developers” in the supplied Java curriculum?
questions.explanation: The supplied PDF lists “Threat modeling basics” under lesson 297, “Security Fundamentals for Java Developers”.

questions.prompt: Which approach best supports reliable work with security fundamentals for java developers?
options: Validate data at a trust boundary, keep secrets out of logs, and use vetted platform APIs.
Assume the first successful run proves the code is correct.
Change several unrelated parts until the output looks plausible.
Ignore runtime/version requirements if the code looks familiar.
questions.answer_key: Validate data at a trust boundary, keep secrets out of logs, and use vetted platform APIs.
questions.explanation: Validate data at a trust boundary, keep secrets out of logs, and use vetted platform APIs. A small reproducible test provides stronger evidence than assumption or trial-and-error changes.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest first step when checking an example related to security fundamentals for java developers?
options: State the expected behavior, run or inspect the smallest relevant example, then test one boundary or failure case.
Skip reproducing the behavior and change multiple settings at once.
Trust a screenshot without checking the program or version that produced it.
Disable all validation and error handling.
questions.answer_key: State the expected behavior, run or inspect the smallest relevant example, then test one boundary or failure case.
questions.explanation: State the expected behavior, run or inspect the smallest relevant example, then test one boundary or failure case. This approach makes the result repeatable and helps isolate the cause of a mismatch.
